title: Lesson 76: Cost Architecture: Licensing, API Consumption, Storage, and Optimization
description: The four cost meters in a Salesforce design, how each one is calculated, and which optimization moves actually change the run rate.

questions.question: An Enterprise Edition org has 120 Salesforce licenses, 30 Salesforce Platform licenses, and 800 Customer Community Plus licenses, with no API add-ons. What is the org's daily API request allocation?
questions.explanation: The Enterprise Edition formula is 100,000 base plus licenses times the per-license rate. That gives 100,000 + (120 x 1,000) + (30 x 1,000) + (800 x 200) = 100,000 + 120,000 + 30,000 + 160,000 = 310,000 calls per 24 hours.

questions.question: A nightly integration must upsert 250,000 product records into Salesforce. A developer proposes one REST call per record. Using the lesson's reasoning, what is the correct design and why?
options: Keep the per-record REST design, because the daily request allocation is large enough to absorb 250,000 calls.
Move the load to Bulk API 2.0, because any operation over roughly 2,000 records belongs there and its ingest batches draw from the separate 15,000-batch pool rather than the daily request allocation.
Keep the per-record design but schedule it during business hours so it is metered against interactive user traffic.
Move the load to Platform Events, because event publishes do not count toward any allocation.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that any operation over about 2,000 records belongs in Bulk API 2.0, and that Bulk API has its own separate allocation of 15,000 batches per rolling 24 hours shared with Bulk API, with ingest jobs consuming batches. The cost unit is the call, not the record, so per-record REST turns a modest bulk job into hundreds of thousands of calls.

questions.question: A service agent runs 30,000 conversations a month at four standard actions each in production. Its prompt context carries 6,500 tokens per turn. Using the August 2026 rate card, which statement correctly describes the consumption?
options: Actions cost 120,000 credits and each turn bills one prompt unit, because prompts are billed per request regardless of size.
Actions cost 2.4 million credits, and each turn bills four prompt units because billing rounds up in 2,000-token blocks; trimming context under 2,000 tokens would cut that to one unit per turn.
Actions cost 2.4 million credits, and each turn bills one prompt unit because only input tokens are counted.
Actions cost 600,000 credits, and each turn bills three prompt units because the rate card caps prompts at 6,000 tokens.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives the Standard Action multiplier as 20 in production, so 30,000 conversations x 4 actions = 120,000 actions x 20 = 2.4 million credits. Prompt billing works in blocks of up to 2,000 tokens rounded up, and the lesson's example shows 6,500 tokens metering as four units, while anything under 2,000 tokens bills one unit.
